## Stress has a chemistry too

Brain signaling ([2.1](01-brain-action.qmd)) and brain rhythms ([2.2](02-brainwaves.qmd)) are two windows on tea's dual story. This sitting opens a third: **what happens in the body when the day itself is noisy**.

When you are stressed, the body runs a chemical fire-alarm loop. One main output is a stress hormone many people have heard of: **cortisol**. Another fast "go" signal is adrenaline. You do not need the full loop diagram to follow the story—the foldouts hold it.

## Plain takeaways

Imagine a fire alarm (real stress) and also a loud caffeine "boost" siren.

- Caffeine can push the stress-chemistry loop and raise cortisol.
- With daily caffeine use, that *caffeine-driven* siren often gets quieter over days—but the fire alarm of **real stress** can still ring.[^5]
- L-theanine is studied for helping keep heart rate, blood pressure, stress-linked enzymes, and how stressed people *feel* nearer baseline when the load is on.[^1][^3][^4]

In everyday clothes: habit can quiet the caffeine siren. It does not delete the fire alarm. That is exactly where L-theanine studies earn their keep.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: the stress loop, study table, and honesty notes"}
When you are stressed, the body runs a loop often called the **HPA axis** (brain → pituitary → adrenals). One output is **cortisol**. Another related signal is **epinephrine** (adrenaline). **Salivary alpha-amylase (sAA)** is a stress-linked enzyme often used as a "go-system" marker.

| Measure | Condition | Finding | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heart rate / salivary IgA under arithmetic stress | L-theanine vs placebo | L-theanine reduced heart-rate and salivary immune-stress responses; heart-rhythm pattern suggested less "go" drive | Kimura et al. (2007)[^1] |
| Blood pressure / tension-anxiety under mental tasks | L-theanine vs placebo | L-theanine attenuated BP rise in high-response adults and lowered Tension-Anxiety scores vs placebo | Yoto et al. (2012)[^3] |
| Morning salivary alpha-amylase during stressful practice | ~200 mg L-theanine twice daily vs placebo | Theanine group showed lower pre-practice sAA and lower subjective stress during a multi-day pharmacy practice | Unno et al. (2013)[^4] |
| Salivary cortisol across the day | 250 mg caffeine challenges after controlled intake weeks | After abstinence, caffeine raised cortisol robustly; after ~5 days at 300–600 mg/day, morning challenge responses were blunted but not all-day abolished | Lovallo et al. (2005)[^5] |

**Honesty note: where pack tables and papers diverge**

Some companion pack tables attribute a neat salivary-cortisol delta (L-theanine ~±5% vs placebo ~+22%) to **Yoto et al. (2012)**. The published Yoto 2012 paper measures **blood pressure and mood under stress**, not that cortisol contrast.[^3] This lesson therefore cites Yoto for BP/anxiety, Kimura for HR/sIgA, Unno for sAA under real student stress, and Lovallo for caffeine–cortisol adaptation—and does **not** repeat the mismatched cortisol attribution as fact.

Pack tables also sometimes phrase caffeine–cortisol adaptation as "nearly gone within five days." Lovallo's controlled trial is more precise: after five days at 300 or 600 mg/day, the **morning** caffeine-challenge cortisol response was largely abolished, but cortisol could still rise later in the day after further doses—**reduced, not eliminated**.[^5]

**Vessel tone.** Caffeine can constrict cerebral vessels as part of its sleepy-signal blockade story.[^7] L-theanine has been shown in cell work to promote nitric-oxide production in endothelial cells—one plausible path for "steadier pressure" language.[^2] Yoto's human stress design adds a bridge: L-theanine can blunt task-related blood-pressure climbs in high-responders.[^3] That is mechanism-plus-trial talk, not a home blood-pressure prescription.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Before you believe a stress headline:** check **dose**, **task vs rest**, **timing**, and **what was compared**—the same four questions Module 2.2 teaches for brain-wave claims.
:::

## Myth check: "Caffeine permanently wrecks your adrenals"

Acute caffeine can raise cortisol a lot. With daily use in the hundreds of milligrams, that caffeine-driven spike often shrinks within about five days of controlled intake—but the careful trial says **incomplete** quieting at everyday levels, not permanent adrenal destruction and not a total mute button.[^5] Stress-driven responses can still rise, which is exactly where L-theanine studies (Kimura, Yoto, Unno) earn their keep.[^1][^3][^4] Systematic reviews of L-theanine and stress/anxiety stay cautious: effects exist in some trials, but dose, setting, and what you measure matter.[^6]

## A bridge into Chapter 4

This hormone thread also reaches forward into Chapter 4: when stress chemistry rises, people can become more aggressive risk seekers in some lab settings. Softened loss aversion under pressure is one of the bridges on the [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd) page.

Hormones are still somewhat invisible. What can you see on the outside of the body?

## Story in one minute

Stress runs a chemical fire-alarm loop toward cortisol and related signals. Caffeine can push that loop; habitual intake blunts caffeine-driven spikes incompletely. L-theanine is studied for keeping heart rate, blood pressure, stress enzymes, and subjective stress nearer baseline under load. Pack tables that mis-attribute cortisol numbers to Yoto 2012 are corrected here: Yoto is blood pressure and mood; Lovallo is caffeine–cortisol adaptation.

::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- Stress has a chemistry: a fire-alarm hormone story, not only a mood word.
- Caffeine can raise the siren; L-theanine-linked drinks more often keep markers nearer baseline in cited designs.
- Before you believe a stress headline: **dose, task, timing, contrast** (same literacy as Module 2.2).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: what this means when you drink tea"}
- "I adapted to coffee" ≠ "stress no longer raises cortisol."[^5]
- L-theanine stress findings are often **task** or **real-life stress** designs—not magic on a sofa.[^1][^4]
- Vessel and blood-pressure talk is supportive physiology, not a treatment plan.[^2][^3]
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: which paper answers which question?"}
| Question | Better primary trail |
| --- | --- |
| Does L-theanine reduce HR / stress markers under acute lab stress? | Kimura et al. (2007)[^1] |
| Does L-theanine blunt BP / tension under mental tasks? | Yoto et al. (2012)[^3] |
| Does multi-day theanine change sAA / subjective stress in real student stress? | Unno et al. (2013)[^4] |
| Does daily caffeine blunt caffeine-driven cortisol? | Lovallo et al. (2005) — reduced, not eliminated[^5] |
| Do reviews stay cautious? | Williams et al. (2020)[^6] |

Keeping the question matched to the paper is how this course stays honest when secondary tables blur together.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: take-home checklist for Lesson 2.3"}
1. Stress loop → cortisol; caffeine can push it (HPA axis in the foldout above).
2. Habituation ≠ zero stress chemistry.[^5]
3. L-theanine evidence is marker- and setting-specific.[^1][^3][^4]
4. Correct pack/paper mismatches when you see them (Yoto ≠ that cortisol delta).
5. Next: body meters you can measure without a hormone assay.
:::
